In order to help us see the resulting pattern, iso-sensitivity contours have been added to show sets of points with the same values of d′: What is immediately clear is that sensitivity has a non-linear relationship with hit rate and false alarm rate. Visualizing the relationship between d′, HR, and FAR Showing the sensitivity for every location in ROC space is instructive, but when we are focused on performance, a more typical approach is to plot a single iso-sensitivity curve through our data point. This curve shows all of the combinations of hit rate and false alarm rate that have the same sensitivity as our actual data. As the Hit Rate or False Alarm Rate are changed, d′ and c will also change, and thus the Iso-Sensitivity Curve will adjust as well. As a result, neither hit rate alone nor false alarm rate alone tells you anything about sensitivity — you need both! results.title: Operating-Characteristic Curve - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: # Operating-Characteristic Curve. An operating characteristic curve, or ROC curve, is defined as a plot that illustrates the performance of a test in distinguishing between two classes by plotting the true positive rate against the false positive rate for various threshold settings. Each point on the curve represents a sensitivity/specificity pair for a specific threshold, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC) serves as a measure of the test's accuracy in classifying the two groups.
